newsitem.title: CAMEROON: Cameroon targets 5.5 pct growth, 3.0 pct inflation.
newsitem.headline: Cameroon targets 5.5 pct growth, 3.0 pct inflation.

text.p: The Central African state of Cameroon is targeting Gross Domestic Product (GDP) growth of 5.5 percent in the coming budget year with inflation of just three percent, according to a draft budget put before parliament.
GDP growth in the 1996 calendar year, the latest period for which official figures are available, was five percent, while inflation was eight percent.

The draft, presented by Prime Minister Peter Musonge Mafany late on Friday, envisaged a 13 percent increase in spending on the 1996/97 budget year, which was to have ended June 30, but which which President Paul Biya has extended by one month by decree.
The prime minister said the government aimed to balance the budget at 1,256.75 billion CFA francs with receipts matching spending.

Economic analysts said a similar plan in the 1996/97 budget year backfired as expected contributions from donors did not materialise, although details were not immediately available. The 1996/97 budget was supposed to balance at 1,113 billion CFA francs.

Biya, who took over from independence president Ahmadou Ahidjo in 1982, seeks reelection in October. He narrowly defeated opposition leader John Fru Ndi in a 1992 election, which the opposition says was rigged.

Biya's Cameroon People's Democratic Rally (RDPC) won a crushing majority in a May 17 parliamentary election, which the opposition says was also rigged. The ruling party holds 109 of the 180 seats national assembly seats.
Fru Ndi's Social Democratic Front (SDF) won 43 seats, the remainder are divided among five other parties.
SDF national assembly members initially spoke of boycotting parliament but took their seats on the advice of Western diplomats.

They walked out of Friday's session denouncing civil rights abuses by the governor and a traditional leader in the English-speaking Southwest Province and threatened to boycott the budget debate if their grievances were not addressed.
State radio reported on June 28 that the budget year extension would run throughout July, with a budget of one twelfth of the 1996/97 allocation.
Officials attributed the delay in the budget debate to postponement of the parliamentary election from March to May.
Cameroon's new parliament did not hold its inaugural session until June 17.
